title: Nappy Lamar, Galladora, leaving music and calling everyone Joe
summary: Guitarist Nappy Lamar on a recording, Alfred Galladora's reading skill that convinced White to quit, and reflections and the 'Joe' story.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: What did he do on that record, did he play banjo, or guitar?

He played guitar, and he, and Pinky Vedakovich, sang a, a little solo, if you'll notice, on the record. Then another one, that played with us, was, oh, what was that fellow's name? Alfred Galladora. I don't know whether you know, Alfred Galladora, but he played, oh, two or three occasions, with us, at the Southern Yacht Club, when we were spotting. And that was as fine a musician, as I ever, bump up the gifts in my life. I've never met a musician, that could, could transpose, any piece of music, that you put up in front of him, and read it off on that saxophone, like that fellow could. He just, he made me feel so insignificant, as a saxophone player, that I realized, right then and there, that it was time for me, to get out of the music business. They had men like that in it, knew what they were doing, and were, in such control of music. And he was, he was a very, very fine musician. All in all, it's been a very, very comfortable, I wouldn't have missed it, for anything in the world. I think if I had it to do over again, I'd do the same thing. Fact is, if I had it to do over again, I might have stayed in music, because I enjoyed it, so much more than anything, I've ever done in my life. I don't play anymore, I've got the horns, but I don't play anymore. It's a funny thing, but neither one of my youngsters have been too particularly interested in learning music. I think they would have liked to have played, but they didn't want to put the effort in it to learn how to play. But it's been very, very enlightening to me, and it's been the friends that I made through playing music. To give you a little instance of that, when we played at the roof garden, we used to meet so many people, and so many people would call me by name, and I'm a very poor individual in remembering names. So I made up my mind one night, I told Monk, I said, Monk, I can't remember these people's names, and I said, I just insult them when I say hi. I said, I'm going to start something here that I hope will get me out of this dilemma I'm in. I said, I'm going to call everybody Joe. Then if I say hi Joe, they'll say, well, that's all right, he calls everybody Joe. He knows who I am, but he calls me Joe, and that's what I did. For years and years, I called everybody Joe. My best friend was Joe to me, simply for one reason, that I met so many people through music, and I could not remember their names. I just couldn't do it. I didn't want to insult them by calling them, just say hi there, so I started calling everybody Joe. Men, women, and children, all alike, were called Joe. It got me out of an awful predicament that I was in. Later on in life, when I went back into the jewelry business, one of the gentlemen that was there, I called him Joe, he called me Joe, and people used to say, I don't understand why you two fellas got together, and both of your names are Joe. But, well, I guess there's a lot of other experiences that I could relate, if I could only think of them. I know, you know.
